subject: Human Performance
question_text: Why is hypoxia particularly dangerous for a pilot?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its early effects impair judgement, so the pilot may not recognise it

choices.label: B
choices.text: It always causes severe pain before any loss of performance

choices.label: C
choices.text: It only occurs above 25,000 ft

choices.label: D
choices.text: It can be cured by drinking water

explanation: Hypoxia often causes euphoria and impaired judgement before obvious symptoms appear. Pilots may not notice their own deterioration, so they need to know their own symptoms and use oxygen as required.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Hypoxia is usually painless and insidious.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Night vision is affected from about 5,000 ft, and performance degrades progressively above roughly 10,000 ft.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Only supplemental oxygen or descent restores oxygen supply.

subject: Human Performance
learning_objective: Identify the cause and remedy of hyperventilation
question_text: A nervous pilot feels dizzy, with tingling fingers and lips, while breathing rapidly at low altitude. What is the likely cause and correct action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypoxia; climb to a higher altitude

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hyperventilation; consciously slow the rate and depth of breathing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning; breathe faster

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decompression sickness; descend immediately

explanation: Over-breathing removes too much carbon dioxide, causing dizziness, tingling and cramps. Slowing the breathing (for example by talking or breathing into a cupped hand) restores CO2 levels.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: At low altitude with rapid breathing, hypoxia is unlikely, and climbing would make any hypoxia worse.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Breathing faster does not treat CO poisoning; fresh air and turning off the heater do.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Decompression sickness at low altitude, without recent diving, is very unlikely.

handbook_reference: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C, public domain), chapter: Aeromedical Factors / Aeronautical Decision-Making

subject: Human Performance
question_text: A pilot using the cabin heater develops a headache and drowsiness, and suspects carbon monoxide. What is the most appropriate action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase cabin heat to stay alert

choices.label: B
choices.text: Climb to a higher altitude to improve ventilation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn off the cabin heat, open the fresh-air vents and land as soon as practicable

choices.label: D
choices.text: Continue the flight; symptoms will clear by themselves

explanation: Exhaust gas leaking through a heat exchanger can bring CO into the cabin. CO binds to haemoglobin far more readily than oxygen, so remove the source, ventilate, and land.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The heater is the probable source of the CO.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Lower air pressure at altitude makes the hypoxic effect of CO worse.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: CO binds strongly to haemoglobin, and exposure must be stopped.

subject: Human Performance
learning_objective: Explain the risk of flying after scuba diving
question_text: What is the main risk of flying shortly after scuba diving?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hyperventilation from the cold water

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ear barotrauma during the climb only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning from the air tanks

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decompression sickness, from nitrogen absorbed while diving forming bubbles at lower cabin pressure

explanation: At depth the body absorbs extra nitrogen. Reducing the ambient pressure too soon, for example in a climb, can let it come out of solution as bubbles, causing the bends. Pilots should wait the recommended interval before flying.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The diving risk is caused by dissolved nitrogen, not breathing rate.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Ear problems are possible, but the main hazard is decompression sickness.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: CO is not the recognised risk of flying after diving.

question_text: What speeds up the removal of alcohol from the body?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nothing; only time removes it

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drinking strong coffee

choices.label: C
choices.text: Breathing 100 percent oxygen

choices.label: D
choices.text: A cold shower and exercise

explanation: The liver removes alcohol at a roughly constant rate. Coffee, oxygen, showers and exercise do not change it, and effects can persist well after drinking stops.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Caffeine may make a person feel more alert but does not lower blood alcohol.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Oxygen does not speed up the metabolism of alcohol.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: These do not meaningfully increase the rate at which the liver removes alcohol.

subject: Human Performance
learning_objective: Identify when ear barotrauma is most likely
question_text: A pilot with a heavy cold is flying. During which phase are painful ear blocks most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During climb

choices.label: B
choices.text: During descent

choices.label: C
choices.text: In level cruise

choices.label: D
choices.text: While taxiing

explanation: On descent, air must flow back into the middle ear through the Eustachian tube. A swollen tube from a cold can stop this, causing pain and possibly a ruptured eardrum.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: During climb, air escapes from the middle ear relatively easily.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Pressure is constant in cruise, so there is no pressure difference to equalise.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: No significant pressure change occurs on the ground.

subject: Human Performance
question_text: During a rapid acceleration after take-off in poor visibility, what false sensation may the pilot experience?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A nose-down pitch, which may tempt the pilot to pull up

choices.label: B
choices.text: A roll to the left

choices.label: C
choices.text: A nose-up pitch, which may tempt the pilot to lower the nose

choices.label: D
choices.text: A feeling of tumbling end over end

explanation: The otolith organs cannot tell linear acceleration from a tilt. Forward acceleration feels like a nose-up attitude. Without visual references the pilot may push forward towards the ground.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Deceleration, not acceleration, gives a false nose-down sensation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Linear acceleration is felt as pitch, not roll.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: That is typical of the Coriolis illusion caused by head movement in a turn.

subject: Human Performance
question_text: A pilot in a prolonged turn in cloud quickly moves their head to pick up a chart. What may this cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The illusion of a nose-up pitch

choices.label: B
choices.text: Improved orientation through the semicircular canals

choices.label: C
choices.text: Empty-field myopia

choices.label: D
choices.text: A strong tumbling or rotating sensation (Coriolis illusion)

explanation: During a steady turn the fluid in the semicircular canals stops moving relative to them. A quick head movement in another plane stimulates several canals at once, causing a violent, disorienting sense of rotation.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: That is the somatogravic illusion from linear acceleration.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The head movement produces a false sensation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: That is a visual focusing effect, not a vestibular illusion.

question_text: On approach to an upsloping runway, what illusion may the pilot experience and what is the risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The aeroplane appears too high, so the pilot may fly a lower approach than intended

choices.label: B
choices.text: The aeroplane appears too low, so the pilot may fly a higher approach than intended

choices.label: C
choices.text: The aeroplane appears too fast, so the pilot may slow down dangerously

choices.label: D
choices.text: Runway slope causes no visual illusion

explanation: An upsloping runway looks longer and steeper, as if seen from above the normal glidepath. A pilot who corrects for this ends up too low.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: That applies to a downsloping runway.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Runway slope mainly affects the perceived approach angle.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Slope changes the runway's apparent shape and so the perceived glidepath.

subject: Human Performance
question_text: A pilot used to narrow runways approaches a much wider runway than usual. What may they perceive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: That they are higher than they actually are, leading to a low approach

choices.label: B
choices.text: That they are lower than they actually are, leading to a high approach

choices.label: C
choices.text: That the runway is further away, leading to a late flare

choices.label: D
choices.text: No illusion, because width does not affect perception

explanation: A wide runway fills more of the field of view, as a familiar runway would from a lower height. The pilot may then fly a high approach and flare late.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: That applies to a narrower-than-usual runway.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Width mainly affects the perceived height on approach.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Pilots judge height partly from the runway's apparent width.

subject: Human Performance
question_text: At night, how should a pilot look for a dim object?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stare directly at it with the central vision

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn the cockpit lighting to full brightness

choices.label: C
choices.text: Look slightly to one side of it rather than straight at it

choices.label: D
choices.text: Close one eye to improve focus

explanation: At night the rods, which lie outside the central fovea, do most of the seeing. Looking slightly off-centre brings a dim object onto the more sensitive peripheral retina.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The fovea has few rods and is poor in low light, so a dim object can disappear when looked at directly.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This does not improve low-light vision.

question_text: For a person adapted to a normal day-night routine, when is alertness typically lowest?

subject: Human Performance
question_text: How is a pilot's performance related to arousal (stress) level?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Performance always improves as arousal increases

choices.label: B
choices.text: Performance is best when arousal is as low as possible

choices.label: C
choices.text: Performance is best at a moderate level of arousal and worse when arousal is too low or too high

choices.label: D
choices.text: Performance does not depend on arousal

explanation: The relationship is an inverted U (Yerkes-Dodson). Too little arousal leads to inattention, too much to overload and tunnel vision. Performance peaks in between.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Very high arousal narrows attention and degrades performance.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Very low arousal brings boredom and inattention.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Arousal has a well-established effect on performance.

subject: Human Performance
question_text: How does regular cigarette smoking affect a pilot's tolerance of altitude?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It raises tolerance, because the lungs adapt to lower oxygen

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has no effect at the altitudes flown by light aircraft

choices.label: C
choices.text: It lowers tolerance, because carbon monoxide in the blood reduces its oxygen-carrying capacity

choices.label: D
choices.text: It only affects hearing

explanation: Carbon monoxide from smoking binds to some of the haemoglobin. That leaves less to carry oxygen, so a smoker experiences hypoxic effects at a lower altitude than a non-smoker.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Smoking reduces, not improves, oxygen transport.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The effect is noticeable even at moderate altitudes, for example on night vision.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The main altitude-related effect is on oxygen transport.
